readerTitle: Why Adidas stopped trusting its best-looking ads
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Adidas의 2019년 공개 발언) + 실제 연구 (Binet & Field, IPA) + 가상 적용 (피자 가게, 건축가용 소프트웨어)
insight: 클릭과 주문으로 바로 측정되는 광고는 이미 생긴 수요를 거두고, 브랜드 광고는 미래의 수요를 만든다. 대시보드는 앞의 것만 보여준다.
misconception: 성과가 바로 측정되는 광고가 효과도 가장 좋다. 측정되지 않는 브랜드 광고는 돈 낭비다.

sources.text: Marketing Week (2019). Adidas 글로벌 미디어 책임자 Simon Peel의 발언: 디지털·퍼포먼스 마케팅에 과잉 투자했다는 인정
Binet, L. & Field, P. (2013). The Long and the Short of It. IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising).
피자 가게와 건축가용 소프트웨어 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Adidas 사례: Simon Peel이 2019년 Marketing Week 등에서 디지털 퍼포먼스 마케팅에 과잉 투자했고, 계량경제 모델링(econometrics) 결과 브랜드 활동이 도매·매장·온라인 전반의 매출을 이끌고 있었다고 말한 내용. 보도마다 인용된 비율(퍼포먼스 대 브랜드 예산 비중, 브랜드가 만든 매출 비중)이 있으나 확실하지 않아 카드에 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 원문 기사와 날짜를 게시 전 확인하세요.
Binet & Field(2013): IPA 효과성 데이터베이스의 캠페인을 분석해 단기 판매 효과는 빨리 사라지고 브랜드 효과는 느리게 쌓여 오래 간다는 결론. 흔히 인용되는 '브랜드 약 60 : 판매 활성화 약 40' 비율은 평균적 경험칙이며 업종·상황에 따라 다르다고 저자들이 밝힘. 분석 캠페인 수와 비율 표현을 원문으로 확인하세요.
피자 가게와 소프트웨어 사례의 금액·수치는 모두 가상입니다. 계산이 필요한 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why Adidas stopped trusting its best-looking ads
body: For years, Adidas moved more of its budget into online ads that showed clear results: a click, then a sale.
In 2019, its global media director said publicly that the company had **over-invested** in exactly those ads. The dashboards had been telling only half the story.

image.label: A glowing ad dashboard with a shadowy crowd of shoppers behind it
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 앞쪽에 밝게 빛나는 대시보드(클릭, 매출 그래프 상승), 뒤쪽 어두운 배경에 대시보드에 잡히지 않는 매장 안 쇼핑객 무리. 실제 브랜드 로고, 삼선 무늬, 운동화 상표 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your pizza place has $2,000 a month for marketing.
body: Half goes to delivery-app ads. You can see every order they bring. The other half sponsors the local youth football league and a sign by the main road. You can't trace a single order to it.
A friend says: put it all where the orders are. What do you do?

options.text: Move the whole budget to delivery-app ads
options.feedback: You gain spending you can measure. But you may lose the reason people think of you before they open the app at all.

options.text: Keep a steady share in the local sponsorship and judge it over months, not days
options.feedback: You accept less precise measurement in return for staying known in town. The next cards explain why that trade often pays.

options.text: Keep the sponsorship only if customers mention it when they order
options.feedback: A sensible check, but few people can say why a name came to mind. You'd likely undercount its effect.

cards.title: The clicks were taking credit.
body: Adidas tracked online ads click by click, so they looked highly efficient. Brand ads, like big campaigns and sponsorships, looked vague by comparison.

When Adidas used **econometric modelling**, a statistical method that estimates what really drives sales, the picture changed. Brand activity was driving sales across stores, wholesale partners and its own website. The click-based ads had been claiming credit for many buyers who were already coming.
Adidas said it would rebalance toward brand.

cards.title: Brand building vs direct response
body: **Direct response** marketing asks for action now: click, order, book. Its results show up within days and are easy to count.
**Brand building** makes more people know and like you, so you come to mind when they're ready to buy, maybe months later. Its results are slow and spread out.
One harvests demand that already exists. The other creates the demand to harvest.

image.label: A farmer planting seeds on one side, harvesting on the other
image.brief: 좌우 분할 일러스트. 왼쪽 "Brand building": 넓은 밭에 씨앗을 뿌리는 사람, 작은 새싹. 오른쪽 "Direct response": 다 자란 작물을 바구니에 거두는 사람. 가운데 시간 화살표 "months".

cards.title: Short effects fade. Brand effects build.
body: Les Binet and Peter Field studied hundreds of ad campaigns in the UK's IPA effectiveness database. Their 2013 report, *The Long and the Short of It*, found that sales from direct response ads spike and fade fast. Brand effects grow slowly but last much longer.
Campaigns that combined both did best. Their often-quoted rule of thumb is roughly 60% brand and 40% direct response, though they stress the right mix varies by category.

cards.title: The last click gets the credit.
body: Someone sees your sign by the road for months. One Friday they type "pizza near me" and tap your ad. The ad gets the credit. The sign made the search end with you.
That's why cutting brand work can look harmless for a while. Direct response keeps harvesting what brand already planted. Sales slip later, when it's hard to see why.

image.label: A customer's path: roadside sign, football match, then a phone tap
image.brief: 한 고객의 여정을 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로. 길가 간판 → 유소년 축구 경기 현수막 → 금요일 밤 휴대폰 검색 → 주문. 마지막 단계에만 "Credited" 스탬프. 실제 배달앱 로고 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Brand building needs time, cash and consistency.
body: A business with a few months of cash can't wait a year for brand effects. Early on, direct response may be the only sensible choice.
Brand work also only pays if people remember it. Changing your look, message or name every season wastes most of it.
And "brand" is not a free pass. It still needs testing, just on a slower clock, using signals like searches for your name or new customers arriving directly.

cards.title: Now it's software for architects.
body: Your project tool sells to small architecture firms. Almost all signups come from paid search ads. Over the past year, the cost per signup has doubled as rivals bid on the same words.
Few architects have heard your name. What's your move?

options.text: Raise your search bids to win back the top spot
options.feedback: You keep signups flowing this month, but you pay more to fish in the same small pond as everyone else.

options.text: Keep search, and steadily add brand work architects see, like industry podcasts and talks, tracking name searches over months
options.feedback: You accept slow, fuzzy results in return for more firms looking for you by name, which search rivals can't outbid.

options.text: Run a one-month brand campaign and keep it only if signups jump
options.feedback: Right direction, wrong clock. Brand effects build over months, so a one-month test will likely judge it a failure.

cards.title: Direct response harvests demand. Brand building plants it.
body: Measure each on its own clock, and don't let the easy-to-count half starve the other.
**Try it today:** split last quarter's marketing spend into "asks for action now" and "makes us known." Then note how your customers first heard of you.
